newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU message to Italy on EMU getting louder.
newsitem.headline: EU message to Italy on EMU getting louder.

text.p: The message from Brussels to Rome is getting louder: You are not ready to join the single currency club in 1999.

Although no one says so publicly -- preferring to repeat the mantra that no country has yet failed the test for economic and monetary union (EMU) -- Italy's European Union partners are increasingly telling it that the odds are against it.
The latest signal came on Monday when EU finance ministers sent what by diplomatic standards was a stinging review of the state of Italian government finances.

It followed the European Commission's forecast last month that, with Greece, Italy was one of only two EU countries likely to miss the EMU test of having a public deficit of three percent or less of Gross Domestic Product this year.

Less direct messages have also been sent, including the floating in the media of a scenario in which Italy would be gracefully let down from joining the first EMU wave in 1999 but would be in by the time coins and notes are circulated in 2002.
EU Monetary Affairs Commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy, denying any special plan for Italy, has reminded it publicly that 2002 is still an option.
Rome has reacted sharply to any talk that it will not make the 1999 deadline or that it will allow itself to be treated differently from other countries.
It has pledged to do what it takes to bring its deficit down to the required ratio this year.
But even if it does, it now faces intensified scrutiny of its longer-term plans.

Rome's EU partners have begun warning Italy about its finances next year -- a direct attempt by those worried about Italy's fitness for EMU to underline the Maastricht Treaty's requirement that deficit reductions be sustainable.

Concern about sustainability among Germany's finance officials led to the drafting at the Dublin EU summit in December of a post-EMU stability pact threatening sanctions on countries that backslide from fiscal austerity.

In its forecasts -- widely viewed by financial markets as optimistic -- the Commission said Italy's budget deficit to GDP ratio was likely to balloon to 3.9 percent in 1998, higher than that projected for Greece.
This was based on unchanged policies and Italy has pledged to slash the deficit, but the message was nonetheless there.
Even more direct was Monday's letter to Italy from the EU finance ministers -- one of nine sent to countries with excessive deficits.
It homed in on what is said was the one-off nature of some of the budgetary actions taken by Rome to meet the 1997 test. These had to be replaced with permanent, structural measures, the letter said.

"(The EU) recommends the Italian government achieve in 1998 a further reduction of the government deficit to well below three percent of GDP. Such a step is necessary to secure a durable budgetary adjustment," it said.
In EU-speak to a fellow member state, that is about as blunt as it gets.
